To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Super-resolution radar imaging is possible via convex optimization”.
the angle-delay-Doppier triplets can be resolved at a much finer scale, using ideas from convex optimization.
super-resolution radar imaging is possible by using ideas from compressible sensing, and the super-resolution radar imaging problem can be cast as a convex optimization problem.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1.

the following problem: Given probing signals of finite bandwidth B and finite duration T, received over Nt transmit and Nr receive antennas, can we resolve the angle-delay-Dopppler triplets of objects at finer resolution than 1/B, 1/T, or 1/(NTNr)?

the following problem: given a set of probing signals and the received signal, can we estimate the angle-delay-Dopper triplets and the attenuation factors at a much finer resolution than what standard radars can do?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the resolution is proportional to 2/(NTNR −1) in the angle domain, and 1/√B and 1/T in delay and Doppler domains, respectively.
, if a radar has NT transmit and NR antennas, the delay, angle, and Doppler shift of an object can be estimated at the resolution of 1/(NTN − 1), 1/(NT − 1), and 1/(NR − 1), respectively.

the delay, Dopplers, and angular resolution can be increased by a factor proportional to (NTNR − 0) in delay, by a factor proportional 1/(NT − 0) and 1/(NR − 0), and by a factor proportional T/B in delay, Doppler and angle, respectively, for some 0 > 0.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the resolution of a radar is not limited to 1/B, 1/T, or 1/(NT NR), but can be improved by a factor of 1/(NT − 1) or 1/(NR − 1), depending on which parameter is the most critical one.
the continuous angle, delay, and Doppler resolution of a radar is proportional to ˆ1/(NTNR), 1/(NT − 1), and 1/((NT − 1)/B), respectively.
we can recover a continuous angle-delay-Dopppler triplet at the resolution of 1/(NT − 1), 1/B, and 1/T.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the resolution of standard radarms can be improved by orders of magnitude by exploiting the sparsity of the angle-delay-Doppelr triplets of objects in a scene.
the resolution of a radar is limited not by the physical constraints of the radar, but by the number of measurements it takes.
a single radar with a small number of antennas can achieve super resolution in delay, Doppler and angle, provided the angle, delay and Doppler are separated by a factor proportional to 1/NTNR.
